title: Chapter LVI

teacherSummary.text: Lady Catherine arrives unexpectedly and demands that Elizabeth promise never to marry Darcy, claiming he is engaged to Anne. Elizabeth refuses to promise anything, defending her right to choose.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter LVI,” how does Austen show the great confrontation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the conflict you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter LVI, how does Austen develop the idea of the great confrontation? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the conflict in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter LVI develops the idea of the great confrontation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter LVI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its conflict shape the reader's understanding of the great confrontation. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter LVI suggests about the great confrontation. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's conflict and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses conflict in Chapter LVI to complicate the reader's understanding of the great confrontation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter LVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the great confrontation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter LVI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the great confrontation follows or bends those conventions, using the conflict as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter LVI and its treatment of the great confrontation. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's conflict and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter LVI as evidence for a larger claim about the great confrontation in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter LVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the great confrontation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What gives Elizabeth the courage to defy Lady Catherine? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are dissuaded, upstart, trifled, equipage, patched. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “You are to understand, Miss Bennet, that I came here with the determined resolution of carrying my purpose; nor will I be dissuaded from it.” In this sentence it means: talked out of something. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Aristocratic marriages were often arranged to keep wealth in families. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's defiance is a high point of independence against rank. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for conflict.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Elizabeth obeyed, and running into her own room for her parasol, attended her noble guest downstairs.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the great confrontation? I circle “pronouncing”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find conflict, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for conflict.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of conflict. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Conflict, Characterization, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter LVI develops the idea of the great confrontation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of conflict and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the great confrontation, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how conflict shapes the great confrontation. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
